headline: To betray is to “cut” the “back” — きる voiced to ぎる.

sources.quote: Compound of 裏 (ura, “back, behind”) + 切る (kiru, “cut”). The kiru changes to giru as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: “To think” has a long run of sound changes from kamugapu, and a handful of rival theories for its start.

sources.quote: */kamukapu/ → /kamuɡapu/ → /kanɡafu/ → /kanɡaferu/ (regular change for lower bigrade verbs) → */kangaweru/ (semi-regular sound shift for the /f/ phoneme; see ハ行(ぎょう)転(てん)呼(こ) (ha-gyō tenko)) → /kanɡajeru/ (semi-regular sound shift, collapsing /we/ into /je/) → /kanɡaeru/
From Old Japanese. First cited to the Nihon Shoki of 720.
Ultimate derivation uncertain. Theories include:

Given the ancient kamugapu spelling, may be ka + mukau, where the ka is an unidentified prefixing element, or possibly 処(か) (ka), cognate with the こ (ko) in location determiners like ここ (koko, “here”) and どこ (doko, “where”), and the mukau is 向(む)かう (mukau, “to face something, to face a direction”, pronounced as mukapu in ancient times), from the sense of facing a thing or issue to thoroughly inspect it and think it over. The shift from mukapu to mugapu may be an example of assimilation and lenition, where the preceding /m/ softens the following /k/.

Alternatively, may be derived from the on'yomi of kan for the character 勘(かん) (kan, “intuition, perception”, prior to the development of the kana ん, this was spelled as kamu), plus some unknown element that was probably originally kapu, changing to gapu due to rendaku. The semantically relevant verbs with ancient readings of kapu, such as 変(か)える (kaeru, “to change”) all have to do with ideas of changing or turning, suggesting a possible original meaning of to change one's perception.

In addition, there are also obsolete readings of かうがふ (kaugafu, /m/ elided; compare the change of suffix む (-mu) to う (-u) or the usage of 柑(かん) (kan) in 柑(こう)子(じ) (kōji)), and かがふ (kagafu, /mu/ elided completely, as in man'yōgana or nanori usage of kanji like 安), giving further support for this etymology.

meaning: two days; second day of the month
headline: “Two days” has a ふつ that is not the usual reading of 二.

sources.quote: /putuka/ → /fut͡suka/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720.

Analyzable as a compound of 二 (futsu, “two”, irregular reading, apparently a shift from expected reading futa) + 日 (ka, “day”, uncommon variant only occurring in certain compounds of ancient derivation).

headline: The organ travelled as an “internationalism”, so its immediate source is hard to pin down.

sources.quote: Internationalism; see English organ. Probably from Portuguese órgão or English organ.

headline: To tell is to “narrate a thing” — with かたる voiced to がたる.

sources.quote: 物(もの) (mono, “thing”) + 語(かた)る (kataru, “to tell, narrate”).
The kataru changes to gataru as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: A hint or sign is a “mood crawling around” — spelled with a 配 that was only fitted to the sound.

sources.quote: From earlier けはひ (kefafi), a compound of 気(け) (ke, “atmosphere, spirit; feeling, mood”) + 這(は)ひ (fafi, “creeping, crawling; spreading”, modern 這(は)い (hai); the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 這(は)ふ (fafu, “to crawl, to creep; to spread along the ground, to spread around”, modern 這(は)う (hau))).
The kanji 配 (“distribution”) was applied to the hai portion of the reading as an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

headline: In its older native reading, “young girl” was “little” plus “female” — much as the word for “man” began as “young boy”.

sources.quote: 少女 (shōjo): a girl holding a puppy.
From Middle Chinese compound 少女 (MC syewX|syewH nrjoX|nrjoH). Compare modern Mandarin 少女 (shàonǚ).

headline: “Considerable” is “big” plus a verb that says it's already done.

sources.quote: Compound of 大 (tai, “big”) + した (shita, “did, done”), the perfective of する (suru, “to do”), used here to indicate a state as opposed to an action.

headline: The checkout is a clipped “register”.

sources.quote: Clipping of レジスター (rejisutā), from English register.

headline: “Wonderful” began as “that which makes one shrink away” — a strongly negative word.

sources.quote: Originally derived from 窄(すば)る (subaru, “to shrink, to get smaller”, archaic) + しい (-shii, adjectivizing suffix evoking the quality of the suffixed term), from the sense of “that which makes one shrink away”. Compare verbs 窄まる (subomaru), 窄める (subomeru). The kanji spelling is an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

The initial sense was strongly negative, and this usage continued until at least the mid-1800s in the Edo period, when the meaning shifted to a strong positive instead. Compare the development of English terrific, of strongly positive meanings, from terrify, of strongly negative meanings.
The modern kanji spelling could be considered an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

headline: A jacket is “upper wear”, using a bound form of “up” and a voiced ぎ.

sources.quote: From 上(うわ) (uwa-, 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 上(うえ) (ue, “up; top”)) + 着(ぎ) (-gi, “clothes; -wear”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 着(き)る (kiru, “to wear”)). The ki changes to gi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: A zabuton is a “seat futon”, with ふとん voicing to ぶとん.

sources.quote: Compound of 座(ざ) (za, “seat”) + 布団(ふとん) (futon, “futon”). The futon reading for 布団 changes to buton as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

meaning: to till, to plow, to cultivate
headline: To till a field began as a “field” plus “return”, and the middle of the word has since softened.

sources.quote: Shift from older 田返す (tagaesu/takaesu), from 田 (ta, “cultivated field”) + 返す (kaesu).

headline: The “however” that opens a caveat is a “just” with an emphatic particle on the end.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese ただし, from ただ (tada, “just, but”) + し (shi, emphatic particle).

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: “Nutrition” was spelled two ways until a 1920 institute and a 1926 publication settled it.

sources.quote: Coined or borrowed from Chinese 營養 (yíngyǎng, “to nourish the body”) in the end of the Edo period. Both spellings 栄養 and 営養 were used until the establishment of 栄養研究所 (“the Institute of Nutrition”) in the Home Ministry in 1920 and the publication of 『栄養』 by Japanese scientist Tadasu Saiki in 1926, and thence 栄養 has been mainly used.

headline: “Always” is “constancy” with an adverbial に on the end.

sources.quote: Compound of Old Japanese 常 (tsune, “constancy, permanence, forever”) + に (ni, adverbial particle).

headline: Papa could be English, or German — nobody can say which.

sources.quote: From English papa or German Papa.

meaning: to be visible; -- polite verb meaning 来る (くる) --
headline: “To be visible” began as “see” with a suffix that means “can be”.

sources.quote: From classical 見(み)ゆ (miyu), from 見(み)る (miru, “to see”) + ゆ (-yu, potential/passive suffix).
First attested in the Kojiki of 712.

headline: A boy is a “male child” with a little の in between, first cited in 1711.

sources.quote: Compound of 男 (otoko, “man; male”) + の (no, appositional particle) + 子 (ko, “child”).
First cited to a text from 1711.

headline: A tatami room was named for sitting mats long before tatami floors were common.

sources.quote: A compound of 座 (za, “sitting”) + 敷 (shiki, “spreading, covering”), the stem noun form of verb 敷く (shiku, “to spread or lay out on the floor or ground”).

Japanese houses originally had wood floors, and mats or cushions called 座 (za) would be laid out (敷く (shiku)) for sitting upon. Tatami (畳) flooring did not become common until some time during the Muromachi Period, approximately 1337 to 1573.

headline: A main street is a “large street” — with the 通り voicing to どおり.

sources.quote: 大(おお) (ō-, “large”) + 通(とお)り (tōri, “street”).
The tōri changes to dōri as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Ikebana is “making flowers live” — with the はな softened to ばな.

sources.quote: Compound of 生け (ike, “making something come alive”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 生ける (ikeru, “to make something live”)) + 花 (hana, “flower”). The hana changes to bana as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: The Emperor is the “heavenly sovereign” — and the の is a sound that crept in between.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 天皇 (MC then hwang) with the original sense of “heavenly sovereign”.
The 呉(ご)音(おん) (goon, literally “Wu sound”) pronunciation, so likely the initial borrowing from Middle Chinese. The ō reading for 皇 changes to nō as an instance of renjō (連(れん)声(じょう)).

headline: The merchant's しょうにん is Chinese; the native word looks like “trade-person”, あきびと.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 商人 (MC syang nyin).

headline: “So to speak” is a “say” in a hypothetical form: “if one were to say”.

sources.quote: The Classical Japanese conditional form of the verb 言う (iu, “to say, to speak”): 言わ (iwa, 未然形 (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of the verb 言う (iu)) + ば (-ba, an inflectional suffix indicating the hypothetical condition).

headline: Salad is an internationalism — Wiktionary lists English, French and Portuguese as candidate sources.

sources.quote: Internationalism of uncertain specifics, variously proposed to derive from English salad, French salade or Portuguese salada.

headline: Politely “your daughter” puts an honorific on both sides of a word for an “unmarried woman”.

sources.quote: Of お (honorific prefix) + 嬢 (jō, “unmarried woman; daughter”) + さん (honorific suffix)

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: Work is “doing” plus “thing”, and the 仕 is only ateji.

sources.quote: From し (shi, “doing”, continuative form of する (suru, “to do”)) + 事 (koto, “thing; stuff”). The koto reading for 事 changes to goto as an instance of rendaku (連濁). 仕 is ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).
